docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Local-first, hybrid semantic-lexical recommendation engine for personal media libraries. This is a concise blueprint; the phased build history and per-module detail live in moon/ROADMAP.md and moon/roadmaps/.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
A five-stage pipeline — stages 1–2 run offline (ingestion), stages 3–5 run online (query time).

[Offline]  Raw metadata (JSON/CSV)
             → BGE-M3 embeddings (dense = semantic, sparse = lexical)
             → SQLite store (scalar + JSON-array columns + vector blobs)

[Online]   User prompt
             1. Self-Querying Retriever (LLM) → {semantic_query, SQL WHERE}
             2. Hybrid Retrieval             → cosine(dense) + dot(sparse), filtered by WHERE
             3. Score Fusion (RRF / DBSF)    → + business-logic decay → Recommendation Value
             4. LLM Explainer                → {reasons[], matched_tags[]} per top-K
             5. Output                       → CLI (rich) / JSON

docs.title: Key Design Decisions
docs.text:
• Local-first: SQLite (stdlib) is the vector store — no external services required (infra/global/docker/docker-compose.yml is a placeholder for a possible future backend).
  • Hybrid retrieval: dense (semantic) + sparse (lexical) vectors fused with RRF (default) or DBSF.
  • LLM-optional: Anthropic Claude powers the self-querying parser and the explainer; the engine degrades to deterministic behaviour without an API key (roadmap).
  • Explainability first: every result carries reasons and matched tags derived from item fields.

docs.title: Changed — SQLite migration (replaces Qdrant + JSON-file workflow)
Store layer (src/store.py)
docs.text:
• QdrantStore replaced by SQLiteStore — zero external services required. All item metadata and vectors live in a single .db file (default data/rec_engine.db, configurable via SQLITE_PATH env var).
  • Schema: one items table with native SQLite column types for scalars and JSON TEXT blobs for list fields (genres, tags, associated_entities) and vector fields (dense_vector, sparse_indices, sparse_values).
  • create_collection() — idempotent CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS; returns True on first creation.
  • upsert() — INSERT OR REPLACE with WAL-mode commit per batch.
  • delete() — DELETE WHERE id = ?.
  • collection_info() — SELECT COUNT(*) + db path.
  • fetch_all(where_clause, params) — full rows including vectors (used by retriever for hybrid search).
  • fetch_filtered(where_clause, params, limit) — metadata-only rows without vectors (used for scroll / watch-history profile).
  • In-memory mode: pass sqlite_path=":memory:" for isolated test databases.

docs.title: Retrieval layer (src/retriever.py)
docs.text:
• Qdrant client removed entirely. All vector arithmetic now runs in Python:
  • _cosine(a, b) — cosine similarity for the dense leg.
  • _sparse_dot(idx_q, val_q, idx_d, val_d) — dot-product for the sparse leg.
  • _rrf(ranks) — Reciprocal Rank Fusion (k=60).
  • HybridRetriever.retrieve() parameter renamed qdrant_filter → sql_filter (accepts (where_clause, params) tuple or None).
  • _hybrid_query() — fetches all matching rows, scores both legs, fuses with RRF (default) or DBSF; returns top-K ScoredCandidate list.
  • _dense_only() — cosine-only fallback when sparse vectors are absent.
  • _filter_only() — delegates to store.fetch_filtered() when the semantic query is empty (plan-to-watch-style queries).
  • _payload_to_item() name kept for backward compatibility; semantics unchanged since SQLite column names match the old Qdrant payload keys.

docs.title: Query parser (src/query_parser.py)
docs.text:
• _build_qdrant_filter() replaced by _build_sql_filter() — returns (where_clause: str, params: list) instead of a Qdrant Filter object.
  • Scalar fields (type, watch_status, rating, year_released, num_episodes_or_pages): standard SQL operators (=, !=, >, >=, <, <=, IN, NOT IN).
  • Array fields (genres, tags, associated_entities): json_each() containment checks (EXISTS / NOT EXISTS).
  • parse_to_qdrant() renamed to parse_to_sql() — returns (ParsedQuery, (where_clause, params)).
  • System prompt and few-shot examples unchanged; Claude still produces the same {semantic_query, filters, length_preference_episodes} JSON.

docs.text:
• src/query_parser.py — _call_claude now passes a structured system list with "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"} on the _SYSTEM_PROMPT block. The 3 KB system prompt is transmitted once and cached for 5 minutes, cutting latency and token cost on repeated query-parse calls.

docs.title: Watch-history implicit feedback
docs.text:
• src/schema.py — HistoryProfile Pydantic model:
  • preferred_tags: frozenset[str], preferred_genres: frozenset[str], item_count: int
  • from_payloads(payloads) — builds profile from a list of Qdrant point payloads

  • overlap_fraction(item) — fraction of item's tags + genres that appear in the profile

  • src/config.py — Two new settings:

  • history_min_rating: float (default 7.0) — minimum rating to include in profile

  • history_boost_weight: float (default 0.15) — boost strength (0 = off, 1 = max)

  • src/scorer.py — _history_boost(item, profile):

  • boost = 1 + weight × overlap_fraction(item, profile)
  • Neutral (1.0) when no profile or zero-item count
  • Wired into _rank_one as a fourth multiplicative factor
  • score() now accepts history_profile: Optional[HistoryProfile]

  • 5 new tests in test_scorer.py (empty profile, full overlap, partial overlap, integration with score())

  • src/pipeline.py — _build_history_profile() method:

  • Scrolls Qdrant for items with watch_status in ["watched", "reading"] AND rating >= history_min_rating (max 500 items)
  • Returns None on any error so the pipeline continues without the boost
  • use_history: bool = True constructor flag (disable with --no-history)
  • _store renamed from local store so _build_history_profile can access the client

docs.title: CLI additions (src/cli.py)
docs.text:
• recommend sync --input FILE [--batch-size N] — Incremental upsert: validates input, embeds changed/new items, upserts to Qdrant (UUID-idempotent). Existing items are updated; items not in the file are untouched. Identical flow to ingest without --reset.

  • recommend delete UUID [--yes] — Remove a single item from the collection. Prompts for confirmation unless --yes is passed.

  • recommend query --no-history — Disable the watch-history boost for a single query (useful for comparing results with and without personal feedback signal).

docs.title: Added — Phase 2: Query Parser
docs.text:
• src/cache.py — Thread-safe in-memory LRU cache keyed on normalised (lowercase, collapsed-whitespace) query strings. Prevents redundant Claude API calls for repeated or near-identical queries.
  • src/query_parser.py — QueryParser class wrapping the Claude API (claude-sonnet-4-6 by default). Ships a 10-example few-shot system prompt covering: pure-semantic, pure-filter, mixed NL+structural, manga volumes, CS paper, classic movie, plan-to-watch list, rating threshold, reading status, and short-series-with-genre queries. Outputs ParsedQuery with semantic_query, filters, and length_preference_episodes. _build_qdrant_filter() converts FilterClause objects into Qdrant Filter using must/must_not lists with MatchValue, MatchAny, and Range conditions.
  • Three-layer fallback in QueryParser: missing API key → semantic-only; malformed JSON from Claude → semantic-only; any API/network error → semantic-only. The pipeline never crashes due to a parsing failure.

docs.title: Added — Phase 3: Hybrid Retrieval
docs.text: • src/retriever.py — HybridRetriever class. Issues a single Qdrant query_points call with two Prefetch legs (dense cosine + sparse dot-product) fused server-side with RRF or DBSF (configurable via FUSION_METHOD). Fetches top_k × 4 candidates per leg to ensure the fusion has enough material. Falls back to client.search() with a NamedVector on any Prefetch/fusion error. Supports filter-only scroll when semantic_query is empty (handles plan-to-watch-list style queries with no semantic content).

docs.title: Added — Phase 4: Score Enhancement
docs.text:
• src/scorer.py — Scorer class computing a multiplicative Recommendation Value: rrf_score × rating_boost × recency_decay × length_decay.
  • rating_boost = 1 + log(1 + rating/10) — logarithmic; 10/10 ≈ 1.69×, no rating = 1.0×.
  • recency_decay = exp(-λ × age_years) — configurable LAMBDA_RECENCY (default 0.05).
  • length_decay = exp(-0.5 × ((eps − pref) / scale)²) — Gaussian; only applied when ParsedQuery.length_preference_episodes is set; 1.0 otherwise.
  • Results sorted descending by recommendation_value; 1-based rank assigned after sort.
  • ComponentScores embedded in each RankedResult for transparency.

docs.title: Added — Phase 5: Explainability (XAI)
docs.text:
• src/explainer.py — Explainer class with explain_batch(). Fires all explanations in parallel via asyncio.gather and anthropic.AsyncAnthropic, keeping total latency ≈ single API call. System prompt enforces: cite only provided metadata, no plot spoilers, modality-aware consume verb ("read" vs "watch"), 2–4 reasons, matched_tags must be a strict subset of actual tags. Falls back to a template-based ExplainedResult on any per-item error.
  • Anti-hallucination guard in ExplainedResult.validate_matched_tags() (Pydantic v2 @model_validator): strips any tag in matched_tags not present in the item's actual tags + genres at model construction time.

docs.title: Recommendation Engine — Implementation Roadmap
docs.text: This is the master roadmap. It tracks the phased build-out below; per-module engineering roadmaps live under docs/moon/roadmaps/. Completed items are recorded in docs/CHANGELOG.md. System design is summarised in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.

docs.title: Module Roadmaps
docs.text:
The engine is a five-stage pipeline (src/). Each subsystem has a dedicated roadmap:

Roadmap Modules Scope Ingestion & Data src/data Loading, embedding (BGE-M3), export, SQLite store Search & Retrieval src/search Query parser, hybrid retrieval, fusion/scoring, reranking, explainer CLI & Output src/cli Click CLI, rich output/JSON Core & Infrastructure src/core Config, cache, schema; tooling & quality

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Build a personal, local-first recommendation engine that accepts a dataset of media files with rich metadata and a free-form search prompt (natural language, tags/genres, or both), and returns a ranked list of recommendations with a computed Recommendation Value and a human-readable list of reasons for each result.

Phase scope: Start with videos (anime, shows, movies). Branch into multi-modal (books, manga, papers) once the core pipeline is stable.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
The system is a five-stage pipeline. Stages 1–2 run offline (ingestion); stages 3–5 run online (query time).

[Offline]
  Raw metadata (JSON/CSV)
       │
       ▼
  BGE-M3 embeddings
  ├── Dense vector  → review/notes semantic space
  └── Sparse vector → title + tags + genres + entities lexical space
       │
       ▼
  SQLite database
  (items table: scalar columns + JSON array columns + vector blobs)

[Online]
  User prompt
       │
       ▼
  1. Self-Querying Retriever (LLM)
     └── {semantic_query, SQL WHERE clause}
       │
       ▼
  2. Hybrid Retrieval (Python vector math)
     ├── Cosine similarity on dense vectors  ┐
     └── Dot-product on sparse vectors       ┘ → both filtered by SQL WHERE
       │
       ▼
  3. Score Fusion (RRF default, DBSF optional)
     + Business logic decay
     → Recommendation Value per candidate
       │
       ▼
  4. LLM Explainer
     └── {reasons[], matched_tags[]} per top-K result
       │
       ▼
  5. Output (CLI / JSON)

docs.title: Data Schema
docs.text:
Every item in the dataset conforms to this schema. Fields in bold are indexed in Qdrant as filterable scalar payload. Fields marked [vector] are embedded.

{
  "id": "uuid-v4",                       // stable identifier
  "title": "string",                     // [vector: sparse]
  "type": "anime|show|movie|book|manga|paper|...",  // [bold payload]
  "watch_status": "watched|reading|plan_to_watch|dropped|on_hold",  // [bold payload]
  "rating": 8.5,                         // float 0–10 [bold payload]
  "year_released": 2019,                 // int [bold payload]
  "num_episodes_or_pages": 24,           // int [bold payload]
  "genres": ["Action", "Sci-Fi"],        // string[] [vector: sparse]
  "tags": ["cyberpunk", "time-travel"],  // string[] [vector: sparse]
  "associated_entities": ["Shinichiro Watanabe"],  // string[] [vector: sparse]
  "local_file_location": "/path/to/file",   // unindexed payload
  "web_link": "https://...",                // unindexed payload
  "review_notes": "string",             // [vector: dense]
  // Phase 7 additions:
  "abstract": "string",                 // [vector: dense, papers only]
  "volumes": 12                         // int, manga only
}

review_notes is the primary semantic field. Priority order for dense text: review_notes → abstract → synthesised fallback (title + genres + tags).

docs.title: Phase 3 — Hybrid Retrieval ✅
docs.text: Goal: Execute parallel dense + sparse search against Qdrant, fused with RRF, returning top-K candidates with scores.

docs.title: Search recipe (Python vector math)
docs.text:
rows = store.fetch_all(where_clause, params)   # SQL-filtered rows

dense_scores = [(i, cosine(query_dense, row["dense_vector"])) for i, row in enumerate(rows)]
sparse_scores = [(i, dot(query_sparse, row["sparse_indices"], row["sparse_values"])) for i, row in enumerate(rows)]

# RRF fusion
dense_rank = {idx: r+1 for r, (idx, _) in enumerate(sorted(dense_scores, reverse=True))}
sparse_rank = {idx: r+1 for r, (idx, _) in enumerate(sorted(sparse_scores, reverse=True))}
fused = sorted([(i, 1/(60+dense_rank[i]) + 1/(60+sparse_rank[i])) for i in range(len(rows))],
               key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)[:top_k]

docs.title: Phase 4 — Score Enhancement & Recommendation Value ✅
docs.text: Goal: Transform the raw RRF score into a final Recommendation Value using business logic decay functions.

docs.title: Formula
docs.text:
RecommendationValue = rrf_score × rating_boost × recency_decay × length_decay

rating_boost = 1 + log(1 + rating/10) — A 10/10 item gets ≈1.69×, a 5/10 gets ≈1.41×, no rating gets 1.0×.

recency_decay = exp(-λ × (current_year - year_released)) — configurable λ (default 0.05).

length_decay = Gaussian exp(-0.5 × ((episodes - preference) / scale)²) — only applied when the query parser extracts a length preference; 1.0 otherwise.

docs.title: Key Design Decisions
docs.text:
Why BGE-M3 over separate models? A single model call produces dense + sparse + ColBERT multi-vectors simultaneously. Running separate models (e.g., sentence-transformers for dense, SPLADE for sparse) doubles inference cost and introduces embedding space mismatch.

Why SQLite over Qdrant? For a personal media library (typically hundreds to a few thousand items), in-Python brute-force cosine similarity and dot-product scoring is fast enough — ~10 ms for 1 000 1024-dim vectors. SQLite is stdlib, zero-config, portable, and requires no Docker or external service. The previous Qdrant integration (ACORN/HNSW graph, prefetch API) offered better asymptotic performance at scale, but that scale is irrelevant for personal use. Switching to SQLite eliminates the only runtime dependency that required an external process.

Why RRF as default over DBSF? RRF requires no knowledge of score distributions, is invariant to score scale, and is robust against a weak retriever skewing results. DBSF is available as an override when the score magnitudes carry meaningful signal (e.g., very high-confidence exact title matches should dominate).

Why multiplicative (not additive) final score? An additive formula lets a high rating rescue an irrelevant item. Multiplication ensures that a zero-relevance item (rrf_score ≈ 0) always scores near zero regardless of its rating or recency.

Why async LLM calls for explainability? Explanation generation is the highest-latency stage. Running 10 Claude API calls sequentially would add ~10–30 seconds. asyncio.gather reduces this to the latency of a single call (~1–3 seconds).

docs.title: Open Questions / Future Work
docs.text:
• Visual embeddings for images/art: Phase 7 leaves images as a stub. The correct path is CLIP or VLM2Vec-V2 (which supports text + image + video in a unified embedding space) for items where the primary content is visual rather than textual.
  • Cross-item collaborative signals: The current engine is content-based only. If the library grows large and rating patterns emerge across many items, a lightweight matrix factorisation layer could augment the content-based scores — but this is only worthwhile with 500+ rated items.
  • Watch history as implicit feedback: ✅ Implemented in Phase 9 — HistoryProfile aggregates tags/genres from highly-rated watched items; _history_boost() in Scorer applies a configurable multiplicative boost.
  • Web UI: A minimal FastAPI + HTMX frontend would make the engine accessible without a terminal. Out of scope for current phases.
  • Streaming explanations: The Explainer currently waits for all asyncio.gather tasks; streaming the first result as it arrives would reduce perceived latency for large top_k values.
  • Collaborative filtering layer: Track co-ratings across item types (e.g., users who rated Cowboy Bebop highly also tend to rate Samurai Champloo highly). Requires 500+ items and explicit cross-user signals — not applicable to single-user personal libraries yet.
  • Hyperparameter sweep: Tune RRF k, λ_recency, length_scale against the golden query set to maximise NDCG@10 (see scripts/evaluate.py --rerank).

docs.title: Architecture and Design of Hybrid, LLM-Augmented Recommendation Engines
Introduction to the Modern Recommender Paradigm
docs.text: The architecture of recommender systems has fundamentally transformed over the past decade. The industry has shifted from traditional collaborative filtering and matrix factorization toward highly complex, multimodal, and hybrid vector search infrastructures. The proliferation of large, unstructured, and semi-structured datasets necessitates systems capable of understanding deep semantic context while simultaneously respecting strict deterministic metadata constraints. Traditional collaborative filtering systems rely heavily on the user-item matrix, which encodes individual preferences based on historical interactions.1 However, in real-world applications, this rating matrix is notoriously sparse. This sparsity causes collaborative filtering models to degrade significantly in performance, particularly when confronting the "cold start" problem, wherein new users or newly added items lack the interaction history required to generate meaningful collaborative signals.1 To overcome these intrinsic limitations, advanced recommender systems leverage rich side information and metadata.1 When evaluating a comprehensive dataset—such as one containing video titles, categorical types (e.g., anime, shows, movies), watch statuses, numerical ratings from 0 to 10, release years, discrete durations (number of episodes or pages), genres, granular tags, associated entities (actors, producers, directors), and operational pointers (local file locations, web links), alongside highly unstructured textual reviews and notes—purely collaborative or purely keyword-driven algorithms collapse. Consumers now expect a search prompt to seamlessly process complex, multi-intent queries. A query might combine natural language semantics ("I want a dark psychological thriller with a complex villain") with explicit metadata filters ("released after 2010, rated above 8, minimum 12 episodes"). Satisfying these intricate demands requires a hybrid retrieval mechanism augmented by Large Language Models (LLMs). This framework must synthesize dense vector retrieval for semantic understanding, sparse vector retrieval for exact keyword matching, and dynamic metadata filtering for deterministic constraints. Furthermore, the output must bridge the gap between machine computation and human trust. Modern systems are required to output not just a list of recommendations to watch or read, but a synthesized recommendation value and an explainable list of reasons for the recommendation, mitigating the "black box" nature of deep neural networks.4 This comprehensive analysis details the exhaustive engineering protocols required to design such an engine, encompassing multi-embedding strategies, self-querying retrieval mechanisms, hybrid ranking mathematical formulations, business logic injection via decay functions, and the generation of explainable recommendations.

docs.title: Data Representation and Multi-Embedding Strategies
docs.text: The foundation of any high-performance recommendation engine lies in how its raw data is mapped into a machine-readable vector space. The provided dataset contains highly heterogeneous information: dense continuous variables (ratings), discrete numerical values (years, episode counts), categorical classifications (types, genres, tags), relationship arrays (associated entities), unstructured text (titles, reviews, notes), and static application pointers (local file locations and web links).

docs.title: Mitigating the Modality Gap and Embedding Collapse
docs.text: A naive architectural approach to feature engineering involves concatenating all metadata fields into a single massive string (e.g., "Title: X, Genre: Y, Director: Z, Review:...") and passing it through a single embedding model.7 While operationally simple, this concatenation strategy leads to severe dimensionality explosion and embedding collapse.7 Embedding models, particularly those trained predominantly on standard semantic text, suffer from a profound "modality gap" when forced to average unrelated signals into a single mean-pooled dense vector.7 When a numerical release year and a subjective, unstructured user review are compressed into the same vector space, the resulting embedding loses its discriminative power. The semantic nuances of the qualitative reviews become indistinguishable from the categorical weight of the genres, leading to suboptimal retrieval precision. Instead, state-of-the-art architectures deploy a multi-embedding strategy, where distinct fields are embedded separately and managed through a multi-vector database infrastructure.8 By projecting entities into multiple sub-spaces, the model preserves the expressiveness of each data type.8 For example, the narrative summary and review notes reside in a dense semantic space, while categorical tags and associated entities reside in a sparse lexical space.

docs.title: Foundation Models for Unified Vector Generation
docs.text: To achieve multi-embedding without incurring prohibitive computational costs—such as running separate models for dense and sparse representations—the system can leverage unified foundation models like BGE-M3. The BGE-M3 model is distinguished by its versatility in Multi-Linguality, Multi-Functionality, and Multi-Granularity.11 It acts as a unified foundation capable of simultaneously generating dense vectors (for deep semantic relationships), sparse vectors (yielding token weights analogous to BM25), and multi-vector representations from the same input text.11 The sparse retrieval component of BGE-M3 adds a linear layer and a ReLU activation function following the hidden states to generate lexical weights. The formulation is expressed as: $$w_{qt} \= \text{ReLU}(W_{lex}^T H_q[i])$$Based on the token weights of the query and the passage, the relevance score between them is computed by the joint importance of the co-existing terms: 11 By storing multiple vectors per document—a dense vector for the review/notes, a sparse vector for the title, genres, and associated entities—the system can dynamically route search queries to the most appropriate representation space.

docs.title: Payload Optimization and Deterministic Fields
docs.text: Not all fields require vectorization. Operational pointers, specifically the local file location and web link, do not contribute to the semantic or lexical matching process. Embedding a URL or a local file path introduces noise into the vector space. Instead, these fields must be stored purely as unindexed payload metadata.10 When a document is retrieved during the search phase, the vector database returns these strings as part of the payload, allowing the application layer to render clickable links or file path access directly to the user. Similarly, scalar representations for rating, year released, and number of episodes/pages are preserved as distinct numeric payload fields, enabling exact deterministic filtering and mathematical decay functions.10 Modern vector databases support this through nested fields and Parent Block Join implementations, which intelligently manage multi-vector documents and eliminate duplicate vectors from the same document during -Nearest Neighbor (-NN) searches, thereby drastically reducing storage overhead.15

docs.title: Query Understanding via Self-Querying Retrievers
docs.text: When a user submits a search prompt, it may contain unstructured semantic desires ("mind-bending sci-fi with a plot twist"), explicit filtering conditions ("made in the 90s"), categorical tags ("anime"), or a combination of all three. Relying purely on semantic vector search for numeric or temporal constraints is highly inefficient and prone to hallucination. Dense vectors understand the thematic "vibe" of the 1990s but cannot execute a strict, deterministic mathematical filter for year >= 1990 AND year \<= 1999.17 To bridge this gap and properly handle queries that contain natural language alongside tags and genres, the architecture must implement a Self-Querying Retriever.17 This mechanism relies on a Large Language Model (LLM) to intercept the user's natural language prompt, analyze it against a predefined metadata schema, and autonomously parse the prompt into a semantic query string and a set of structured database filters.17

docs.title: Schema Definition and Attribute Information
docs.text:
The implementation begins by defining the dataset's metadata schema using attribute information descriptors. This step is critical, as it provides the LLM with the context required to map natural language onto exact database columns.18

Metadata Field Data Type Description and Context for the LLM type String Categorical format (e.g., anime, show, movie, book, manga). watch_status String User engagement state (e.g., watched, read, plan_to_watch, dropped). rating Integer Numeric score from 0 to 10 denoting perceived quality. year_released Integer The four-digit release year of the content. number_of_episodes Integer Total episode count or page length for filtering short vs. long formats. genres Array High-level thematic classifications (e.g., Action, Romance). tags Array Granular descriptors and tropes (e.g., cyberpunk, enemies-to-lovers). associated_entities Array Actors, producers, directors, animation studios, or authors.

docs.title: Prompt Construction and Allowed Comparators
docs.text:
The query constructor is powered by a highly capable reasoning LLM (such as GPT-4 or similar foundation models) to ensure exact syntax compliance.18 The LLM is provided with strict rules regarding allowed comparators, preventing it from hallucinating operators that the underlying vector database cannot execute. Standard allowed comparators include $eq (equal), $ne (not equal), $gt (greater than), $gte (greater than or equal to), $lt (less than), $lte (less than or equal to), $in (in array), and $nin (not in array).18 To optimize the LLM's parsing accuracy, the prompt constructor utilizes few-shot learning examples. These examples train the query model to distinguish between queries that require deterministic metadata filtering and queries that are purely semantic. For instance, if a user queries "Recommend some films directed by Christopher Nolan", the few-shot prompt teaches the LLM to extract Christopher Nolan and apply an $in filter against the associated_entities field, leaving a blank or minimal semantic query.18 Conversely, if the user asks for "Films with a similar vibe to Christopher Nolan's dream sequences", the LLM recognizes this as a thematic request and passes the entire string to the vector search without applying restrictive filters.18 When the user inputs a complex prompt: "Show me highly-rated mecha anime from before 2015 that I haven't watched yet, preferably a short series under 26 episodes," the Self-Querying Retriever parses this into a structured JSON payload:

JSON { "query": "mecha giant robots thematic", "filter": { "and": [ { "field": "type", "operator": "eq", "value": "anime" }, { "field": "rating", "operator": "gte", "value": 8 }, { "field": "year_released", "operator": "lt", "value": 2015 }, { "field": "watch_status", "operator": "ne", "value": "watched" }, { "field": "number_of_episodes", "operator": "lte", "value": 26 } ] } }

This dual-pronged payload is subsequently dispatched to the vector database. The semantic query ("mecha giant robots thematic") is vectorized and used to calculate similarity against the dense vectors of the reviews and notes, while the strict filters guarantee that only items matching the categorical, length, and temporal conditions are considered in the candidate pool.17

docs.title: Managing Self-Querying Overhead
docs.text: While exceptionally powerful, self-querying retrievers introduce latency overhead and API cost constraints, as an LLM must process every incoming search query.17 The performance of the self-querying process depends heavily on query complexity and dataset scale. To mitigate this, a multi-stage caching architecture is recommended. This involves session-aware caching, which stores normalized query strings and their resulting structured filters within the scope of a user session.20 If a user refines their search from "highly-rated mecha" to "highly-rated mecha movies", the system retrieves the cached semantic embedding and simply re-applies the new $eq: "movie" filter to the existing candidate set in memory, bypassing the LLM and the embedding model entirely.20

docs.title: Vector Database Selection and Filtering Infrastructure
docs.text: The selection of the underlying vector database dictates the performance boundaries of the entire recommendation engine. The architectural requirements—hybrid search (dense plus sparse), multi-vector fields, and heavy, dynamic metadata filtering based on the self-querying output—narrow the viable options to a select few enterprise-grade solutions.

docs.title: Comparative Database Analysis
docs.text:
When evaluating the market for this specific workload, distinct strengths and weaknesses emerge among the leading platforms:

Database Platform Architecture Focus Hybrid Search Capabilities Metadata Filtering Performance Drawbacks Pinecone Fully managed, serverless cloud database.21 Built-in SPLADE and dense vector combinations.21 Filtering heavily impacts read unit consumption. Does not support nested boolean groups natively.21 High operational cost at scale; restrictive query language for complex RAG.21 Milvus Disaggregated compute and storage optimized for billion-vector scale.21 Requires manual orchestration of hybrid pipelines.21 Highly performant but requires significant boilerplate schema definitions and index management.21 Industrial complexity; demands a dedicated data engineering team.21 Weaviate GraphQL-first architecture.21 Native, seamless BM25 + dense vector hybrid search with configurable fusion.21 Schema-based approach allows for rich, nested filters and aggregations.21 Resource-hungry; memory requirements escalate rapidly beyond 50-100 million vectors.21 Qdrant Rust-based, highly memory-efficient system.21 Query API supports flexible prefetch logic for hybrid staging.14 Industry-leading performance via the ACORN algorithm, which integrates filtering directly into HNSW.21 Requires manual management of sparse embeddings as it lacks built-in vectorization modules.21

For a recommendation engine heavily reliant on filtering disparate metadata fields (ratings, years, episodes, watch status), Qdrant represents the optimal balance of performance and cost. Qdrant is highly optimized for filtered search through its ACORN algorithm, which integrates metadata filtering directly into the Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graph traversal, rather than treating it as a post-processing step.21 Consequently, filtered queries remain incredibly fast even when the specified filters eliminate up to 99% of potential vector candidates (e.g., finding unread manga over 500 pages).21 Qdrant’s payload filtering syntax supports nested must, should, and must_not clauses, effortlessly accommodating the complex boolean logic generated by the LangChain query constructor.14

docs.title: Execution of Hybrid Search Recipes
docs.text: To maximize recall without degrading latency, the database must execute carefully orchestrated hybrid search recipes.20 Relying purely on semantic vectors risks ignoring precise user requirements (like a specific actor or tag), while relying purely on lexical BM25 ignores contextual similarity.

docs.title: The Parallel Fusion Pattern
docs.text:
The classic and most robust architecture for this engine is the Parallel BM25 + Vector pattern.20

  1. Lexical Retrieval (Sparse): The system executes a sparse vector search against the title, tags, genres, and associated entities fields. This mechanism captures high-precision lexical hits, ensuring that if a user searches for an exact anime title or a highly specific tag (e.g., "cyberpunk"), the exact matches are retrieved regardless of semantic overlap.20
  2. Semantic Retrieval (Dense): Simultaneously, the system executes an HNSW dense vector search against the review/notes embeddings using cosine similarity. This leg of the search captures candidates that are semantically relevant to the user's natural language input, even if the exact keywords are missing.20
  3. Pre-Filtering Constraints: Both parallel searches are bounded by the exact structured metadata filters extracted by the Self-Querying Retriever, ensuring no discarded items (e.g., dropped shows or already watched movies) enter the candidate sets.17

To prevent latency spikes, the system caps the retrieval limits () on both sides at a manageable number (e.g., 100 to 200 documents) and enforces a strict timeout.20

docs.title: Field-Aware and Tiered Architectures
docs.text: For datasets heavily reliant on metadata, a Field-Aware Hybrid approach is applied. In this pattern, distinct weights are assigned to lexical and semantic matches across different fields.20 For instance, a lexical match in the title field may be weighted at 0.5, while a semantic match in the review/notes field is weighted at 0.3, and an exact match in the associated entities field is weighted at 0.2.20 Furthermore, to maintain sub-100ms latencies, tiered storage strategies are employed. The Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) indexes are stored entirely in memory or on fast NVMe SSDs, sharded by recency or popularity to ensure that high-traffic "hot" documents are routed to the fastest hardware nodes.20

docs.title: Mathematical Rank Normalization and Score Fusion
docs.text: Once the parallel sparse and dense retrieval streams return their respective top- candidates, the system faces a fundamental mathematical challenge: fusing these disparate lists into a single, cohesive ranking to calculate the final Recommendation Value. Fusing dense and sparse scores directly via a naive linear weighted sum is mathematically unsound. Dense scores, such as Cosine similarity, are bounded (typically ranging from 0.0 to 1.0).14 Conversely, sparse lexical scores generated by algorithms like BM25 are unbounded and can scale infinitely depending on term frequency, document length, and the specific query.14 Summing these raw scores results in the sparse score completely dominating the dense score, destroying the semantic relevance of the retrieval. To normalize these disparate streams, the architecture must employ either Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) or Distribution-Based Score Fusion (DBSF) / Relative Score Fusion (RSF).14

docs.title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
docs.text: RRF is a rank-based fusion technique where the absolute mathematical score or distance of a document is deemed irrelevant; only the ordinal position (rank) of the results in each retrieved list matters.23 RRF considers the positions of results within each query and boosts documents that consistently appear closer to the top across multiple modalities.14 The final score for a document is calculated by taking the reciprocal of its rank, multiplying it by an optional weight, and summing these values across all input lists: Where is the set of rankings for a particular document, is the document's zero-based rank in a specific list, is the assigned weight of the retriever (allowing the system to favor semantic over lexical or vice versa), and is a smoothing constant.14 The constant is typically set to 60 to prevent outlier high ranks in a single weak retriever from disproportionately overpowering the final score.14 RRF is highly robust, memory-efficient, and requires zero knowledge of the underlying score distributions, making it an excellent default strategy.14 However, because it relies purely on rank, it is insensitive to the mathematical "gaps" between documents. If the top document is vastly superior to the second document, RRF treats the difference in relevance exactly the same as the difference between the 50th and 51st documents.24

docs.title: Distribution-Based Score Fusion (DBSF) / Relative Score Fusion (RSF)
docs.text: When preserving the score gaps between highly relevant and marginally relevant documents is essential, DBSF (or RSF) is the preferred algorithm.14 DBSF resolves the scale mismatch by normalizing the actual score distributions of the different retrievers per query before combining them.14 This normalization is achieved using Min-Max scaling or L2 normalization over the retrieved batch. For Min-Max normalization, the formula is: 27 By statistically normalizing both the BM25 and Cosine similarity arrays into a strict $$ range for the specific query context, the system safely aligns the disparate metrics. Once normalized, the values from each pipeline are combined—typically via weighted averaging—producing a cohesive score that respects both rank and magnitude.24 Qdrant natively supports DBSF, applying it when users trust the raw scores of their retrievers.14

docs.title: Business Logic Injection via Decay Functions
docs.text: A comprehensive recommendation engine does not rank content solely based on textual query relevance. To deliver a sophisticated Recommendation Value, the system must mathematically incorporate inherent item quality, recency, and user preferences regarding media length. The dataset contains rating (0-10), year released, and number of episodes/pages. A highly textually relevant anime released in 1980 with a 4/10 rating should mathematically yield to a slightly less textually relevant anime released in 2024 with a 9/10 rating. This critical business logic is injected into the final Recommendation Value using Decay Functions.28 Decay functions modify the normalized hybrid search score by applying a mathematical penalty based on a document's continuous distance from an ideal numeric or temporal origin.28

docs.title: Types of Decay Curves
docs.text:
Three primary mathematical curves govern decay in advanced search engines like Elasticsearch and Qdrant (via custom formula queries) 29:

  1. Linear Decay: Applies a constant penalty as distance from the origin increases. It operates as a straight line to zero, creating a hard boundary.29
  2. Exponential Decay (exp): Drops rapidly from the origin and then slows down into a long tail. This is exceptionally useful for recency boosts where newer content is strictly preferred, but older content is never fully penalized to an absolute zero.29
  3. Gaussian Decay (gauss): Features a bell-shaped curve. It decays very slowly near the origin, drops rapidly in the middle, and then tapers off at a very low value. This is ideal for targeting specific historical eras.29 If a user specifies a desire for "90s movies", the origin is set to 1995. Movies from 1995 receive maximum multiplier value, 1992 and 1998 receive mild penalties, while movies from 1980 or 2010 drop off the bell curve and are severely penalized.31

The decay formula configuration requires four parameters: origin (the ideal point of maximum score), scale (the distance from the origin at which the score reaches the defined decay threshold), offset (a defined grace period around the origin where no penalty is applied), and decay (the multiplier value returned at the scale distance, typically defaulting to 0.5).28

docs.text: For a freshness-aware hybrid recommendation where current content is favored, the system applies an exponential decay on the year_released field. The recency boost is calculated programmatically: 20 Similarly, the number of episodes/pages can be decayed if the user indicates a preference for "short reads" or "bingeable shows" (e.g., placing the origin at 12 episodes with a Gaussian decay to penalize 100+ episode series). The ultimate Recommendation Value () is calculated as a composite multiplication of the DBSF-normalized hybrid text score (), the normalized rating score (), and the temporal/length decay functions ( and ): This multiplicative formulation ensures that the final recommendation score is firmly anchored in semantic relevance but dynamically and fluidly shaped by objective quality, recency, and format constraints.

docs.title: Explainable AI (XAI) and Rationale Generation
docs.text: Presenting a list of titles, links, and numeric Recommendation Values fulfills the fundamental requirement of information retrieval. However, modern recommender applications mandate Explainable AI (XAI) capabilities.5 Users increasingly require transparent, natural language rationales detailing precisely why an item breached the ranking threshold and how it aligns with their prompt.4 Providing these rationales dramatically increases user trust, mitigates algorithmic "filter bubbles," and allows coarse-grained system behavior to be interpreted as fine-grained personalization.33 Historically, explainability in recommender systems relied on rigid, pre-programmed templates or visualization of attention weights.34 However, the integration of Large Language Models directly into the final stage of the recommendation pipeline transforms the engine into a dynamic Contrastive-Explanation Generator.4

docs.title: Architecture of the LLM-Based Explainer (XRec)
docs.text: The explanation generation step is strictly decoupled from the high-latency vector retrieval loop. It occurs asynchronously or via parallel batch processing only on the final top- candidate list that has already been ranked and finalized.3 A paramount challenge in LLM-driven explainability is the propensity for hallucination. If a model generates generic praise ("You will love this movie because it has great acting") or hallucinates plot points that do not exist, it violates the transparency requirement and degrades user trust.6 To strictly ground the generation, the LLM must be provided with an airtight prompt context containing the user's original query, the explicit categorical metadata of the recommended video (genres, tags, associated entities), unstructured evidence (reviews, notes), and the scalar values (rating, year). This is achieved using advanced Meta-Prompting and structured output extraction.37 The system employs a "Reason Generation Prompt" designed to output a structured JSON object containing a short, human-readable rationale and an array of explicitly matched tags.37

docs.title: Prompt Template Architecture
docs.text:
To ensure high-quality rationale generation, the LLM prompt template is structured to enforce logical reasoning 40: You are an expert recommender system explanation engine. Your task is to explain to the user why a specific video or book was recommended based on their query and the item's exact metadata. You must adhere strictly to the provided metadata and avoid hallucinating plot points. [User Query Context] Query: {user_prompt} User Watch Status History: {user_preferences_summary} Title: {title} Type: {type} Year: {year} Rating: {rating}/10 Episodes/Pages: {episodes} Genres: {genres} Tags: {tags} Associated Entities: {entities} Review/Notes: {review_snippet} [Instructions]

  1. Identify the intersecting concepts between the User Query Context and the Item Metadata.
  2. Formulate a 2-3 sentence explanation addressing why this item is a strong match. Explicitly highlight matching tags, genres, or entities.
  3. Provide reasoning if the item differs slightly from the prompt but ranks highly due to a high rating or highly relevant review notes (contrastive reasoning).
  4. Output the response in valid JSON format using the keys "reasons" (array of strings) and "matched_tags" (array of strings).

docs.title: Contrastive Reasoning and LCP Optimization
docs.text: By supplying the LLM with review/notes and granular tags, the system generates nuanced, contrastive explanations.4 For instance, if a user searches for "a psychological horror anime without jump scares", a purely lexical system might discard horror entirely to avoid the term "scare". However, the hybrid semantic system correctly retrieves a high-ranking psychological thriller. The LLM then explicitly addresses this nuance in its generated rationale: “While 'Perfect Blue' is broadly classified under the 'horror' genre tag, the user reviews note that it relies on psychological tension and surrealism rather than jump scares, perfectly matching your prompt. Furthermore, its exceptionally high rating (9/10) and direction by Satoshi Kon—an entity you have highly rated previously—make it a premier recommendation.” 33 To continually refine these prompts, systems employ frameworks like Large Context Prompting (LCP), where the LLM is periodically tasked with comparing good explanations against poor ones to identify failure reasons and iteratively optimize the underlying template.38

docs.title: Evaluation Frameworks and System Tuning
docs.text: Deploying a complex, multi-stage hybrid engine requires rigorous evaluation across both offline mathematical metrics and online human-centric metrics.42

docs.title: Offline Ranking Metrics
docs.text: The retrieval and fusion algorithms are evaluated using standard Information Retrieval metrics. The Mean Absolute Error (MAE) measures the average deviation between the system's predicted recommendation value and the user's actual post-consumption rating, providing insight into scoring accuracy.42 To evaluate the ranking quality—ensuring the best items appear at the very top of the list—the system uses Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG).14 By testing the pipeline against a "golden query set," engineers can tune the fusion weights ( in RRF) and decay function scales to optimize NDCG@10.14

docs.title: Online XAI Metrics
docs.text:
Evaluating the LLM-generated list of reasons requires distinct human-centric criteria. User feedback is collected via Likert scales across four primary dimensions 46:

  1. Persuasiveness: Does the generated explanation convince the user to consume the content?
  2. Transparency: Does the explanation clearly articulate the connection between the user's prompt and the item's metadata?
  3. Accuracy: Is the rationale factually consistent with the item's actual attributes and the user's true interests?
  4. Satisfaction: Does the explanation enhance the overall user experience? 46

This feedback loop is utilized to fine-tune the LLM through Reinforcement Learning with Explainable Quality Reward (EQR) models. The EQR models optimize the LLM's output to maximize transparency and satisfaction, ensuring the engine consistently generates fluent, diverse, and highly personalized rationales.5

docs.title: End-to-End System Request Flow
docs.text:
Synthesizing the discussed architectures yields a highly robust, low-latency recommendation pipeline capable of satisfying all required inputs and outputs. The operational flow occurs sequentially:

  1. Ingestion and Embedding Pipeline (Offline):
  2. Content data is ingested into the system.
  3. Categorical fields (tags, genres, associated_entities) are tokenized.
  4. The BGE-M3 model generates dense embeddings for the unstructured review/notes and sparse embeddings for the categorical text.11
  5. The vector data is written to Qdrant. Scalar fields (year_released, rating, number_of_episodes, type, watch_status) and operational payloads (local_file_location, web_link) are indexed as filterable and retrievable metadata.10
  6. Query Parsing (Online - Step 1):
  7. The user submits a prompt containing natural language and/or tags.
  8. The LangChain Self-Querying Retriever parses the prompt via an LLM, generating a clean semantic query string alongside structured JSON metadata filters.17
  9. Hybrid Retrieval (Online - Step 2):
  10. The semantic query string is vectorized into dense and sparse representations.
  11. The vector database executes parallel -NN searches. The dense leg evaluates cosine similarity against reviews; the sparse leg evaluates BM25 lexical overlap against titles and tags.14
  12. Both search legs are strictly confined by the structured filters to ensure deterministic accuracy.
  13. Rank Fusion and Scoring (Online - Step 3):
  14. The top- results from both legs are fused using Distribution-Based Score Fusion (DBSF) or Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) to normalize the disparate bounds of cosine and sparse scores.14
  15. The normalized baseline scores are mathematically multiplied by Gaussian or Exponential decay functions derived from the year_released and number_of_episodes, and logarithmically boosted by the rating.20
  16. The unified list is sorted by this final Recommendation Value.
  17. Explainability Generation (Online - Step 4):
  18. The top-tier finalized documents are packaged with their raw metadata and the user's original query.
  19. This package is passed to an asynchronous LLM using the Reason Generation Prompt Template.38
  20. The LLM autonomously outputs human-readable reasons and an array of explicitly matched_tags.
  21. Response Delivery (Online - Step 5):
  22. The application layer receives the finalized JSON payload.
  23. The UI is rendered, displaying the required outputs: a list of recommendations, direct access pointers (local_file_location and web_link), the computed Recommendation Value, the LLM-generated list of reasons, and the highlighted matching tags.

By transitioning from single-modality algorithms to an orchestrated pipeline of specialized AI and infrastructure components, the system successfully bridges the unpredictability of human language with the deterministic constraints of database architecture. The integration of unified foundation embeddings, self-querying retrievers, mathematically sound rank fusion, and LLM-driven contrastive explanations yields an expert-level recommendation engine that is transparent, highly accurate, and deeply personalized.
